placement.notes: Keep it just out of the patch of direct sun.

light.notes: Bright, indirect light. An hour or two of gentle morning sun is fine; a few hours of strong direct sun can scorch the leaves. In low light, growth slows and new leaves come in without splits.

watering.how_to_check: Lift the pot right after a thorough watering to learn its full weight. Water again when it feels clearly lighter.
watering.how_to_water: Bottom water: stand the pot in a tray of water until the surface soil turns damp. If it is still dry after 15-20 minutes, finish by watering from the top. Do not leave the pot standing in water afterwards. Once a month, water from the top until it drains out the bottom, to flush out fertilizer salts.

soil.notes: Pumice can replace perlite. Prefer coco coir over peat as the more sustainable choice. The bottom-watering mix holds more coir so water wicks up more easily; sources do not pair mixes with watering styles, this pairing is ours.

fertilizer.dilution: Label strength for houseplant fertilizers; 1/2 to 1/4 strength for general all-purpose ones.
fertilizer.notes: Alternative: feed at about 1/4 strength every time you water. If the plant puts out no new growth in winter, pause feeding until spring.

consensus: Bright, indirect light; long periods of direct sun scorch the leaves.
Let the top of the soil dry before watering again, and never leave the pot standing in water.
A chunky, well-draining mix of coir, bark, and perlite or pumice.
Feed a balanced fertilizer while the plant is actively growing.
disputed: PPFD targets come from grow-light vendors. Extension services give only foot-candles or descriptions, and some of those figures convert to a much lower PPFD (Illinois Extension's 'high light' of 300 fc is roughly 60 µmol/m²/s in sunlight).
Winter watering: most sources say every 10-14 days; Epic Gardening says cold spells can cut it to about once a month.
Winter feeding: Penn State feeds monthly through winter; RHS and Iowa State feed only during active growth.
Mix proportions: Soltech and Elm Dirt use mostly bark; Sydney Plant Guy uses equal parts coir, bark and perlite.
